lesson_title: Transforming Triangles and Tracking Vertex Coordinates
hook_text: Same size, same spot — and the warehouse manager still said it was wrong. Here is how the coordinates proved it.
clip_script:
A sign-writer in Durban cuts a triangular arrow stencil to paint direction markers on the floor of a warehouse. The job sheet asks for one marker slid 6 units left. He paints it, and the next morning the manager phones: the right-angle corner is at the tip, not the tail.

He reads the painted corners off the floor plan. Every x negated, every y the same — a reflection in the y-axis, not a translation. Walk the corners round: the original goes anticlockwise, the painted one clockwise. Reversed orientation means a flip. He had turned the stencil over instead of sliding it. Same rule for every vertex, primes on every label, and orientation tells a flip from a slide.
visual_style: A warehouse floor plan with grid lines; a triangular arrow stencil slides and then flips, with arrows circling each triangle's corners to show clockwise versus anticlockwise
